items.content:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

We’ve trained Claude to flag potential misuse in conversations, a technique we call self-assessment. Right after it responds, Claude gives a preliminary safety assessment of the conversation. 

Since we began using self-assessment in June, it has surfaced misuse that our other safeguards weren’t designed to catch.

items.title: Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped u
items.content:
Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.

Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.

To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.

To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.

In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.

As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene. 
https://t.co/dIYP7B1GlD

New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety t
items.content:
New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor.

These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior.

Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute.

Read the full post on the Alignment Science Blog: https://t.co/24Gs1oSw7Q

Tout cela est correct. Merci.

Sauf une chose : j'ai bien créé FAIR en 2013, y compris la branche parisienne en 2015, et montréalaise en 2017.
Mais j'en ai quitté la direction en 2018 pour devenir Chief AI Scientist: je me suis refocalisé sur la recherche (Self-Supervised Learning, JEPA, World Models, etc).
@AntoineBordes et @joellepineau étaient les co-directeurs de 2018 à 2023, jusqu a ce qu'Antoine parte pour Helsing et que Joëlle prenne la direction de FAIR.

Je n'ai jamais été impliqué dans les LLMs, ni pour la recherche (à FAIR), ni pour le développement (qui était dans le groupe de produit GenAI). J'applaudissais des gradins.

Mes seules contributions aux LLMs ont été de défendre Galactica (en octobre 2022) contre les attaques aux vitriol de la twittersphere, de promouvoir le projet Llama en interne (développé par une douzaine de chercheurs à FAIR-Paris, dont @GuillaumeLample et Timothée Lacroix), d'aider à convaincre Mark Zuckerberg de créer un groupe de produit autour de Llama (GenAI, créé début 2023), et de convaincre la direction de distribuer Llama-2 en open source/open weight.
Je n'étais pas du tout impliqué dans la direction de GenAI après sa création, préférant travailler sur la prochaine révolution: l'IA physique.

Si vous cherchez un responsable pour le déception qu'a été Llama-4, c'est plutôt la pression de sortir un produit (trop) rapidement, qui a conduit à un excès de conservatisme et un manque d'innovation de la part de l'équipe de GenAI. 
Mon avis est que l'équipe aurait dû prendre un peu plus de temps et intégrer les dernières techniques venant de la recherche à FAIR.
Mais ils n'en ont pas eu le loisir.

En particulier, conserver plus de pouvoir de décision quant aux choix techniques dans les mains des créateurs originaux de Llama à Paris, au lieu de déplacer les décisions à Menlo Park, aurait peut-être permis de conserver les meilleurs talents un peu plus longtemps et de produire de meilleurs résultats.

items.content:
wildwood is a true marvel of human artistry, craftsmanship, and storytelling. i honestly found it even better than You Can See Everything (gasp!).

[spoilers if you read on]

an interesting trend in both wildwood and hoppers is how they handle death. they’re both movies for young people that treat death as inevitable and natural, and both expose the audience to a surprising amount of it. this feels quite different from the cleaner moral universes of much of modern disney and pixar.

both movies also have strong themes of non-intervention. of course, this is environmentally motivated, but there’s a broader Buddhist / Taoist morality running through both films: the world has a natural balance, and our attempts to impose our own ideas of goodness upon it can be destructive.

this feels quite different from the more Christian-inflected morality of overcoming evil. in these films, nature isn’t inherently good or evil, and trying to eliminate everything we perceive as bad can itself be the source of harm.

i wonder if this reflects a broader generational shift toward stories where it’s increasingly difficult to know what’s “right” or “wrong”, and where good intentions aren’t enough to make an action good.

both films feel like spiritual siblings to princess mononoke, questioning the hubris of humans who believe they can impose their will on the natural world.

wildwood is also visually spectacular and a complete and utter artistic achievement. it is always so rewarding to see fresh new takes on what a movie can be and how stories can be told.

huge fan, go see it!

items.content:
Deepseek just revealed every AI agent secret

Incredibly important article to read if you're building anything AI agent related

Here's basically everything you need to know about building a Grok Bot quality AI agent:

1. Agents are split between routers and workers. The user talks to the router, then gives the work to the workers. The router never does work. This is why the chief of staff model in Grok Bot works SO well

2. Proactive means acting on events, not chats. The agent should always be watching for events and react based on every event that comes through it. Routing to the right worker/action

3. Messages should be in a queue. Users should be able to send messages even while the agent is working, and each message queues/steers the agent

4. Besides the router and workers, there should be a watchdog layer. The watchdog makes sure the agent is always up and fixes it when there are issues. This is why Hermes succeeded and OpenClaw struggled. Constantly broke and couldn't fix itself

5. Protect human attention. Only message the user when it needs to act or the user can use the result. Lighten their cognitive load. Another thing Grok Bot is excellent at. When you message it you can be confident the next message you get will be it saying the task is complete.

Carve off an hour and read this incredible article

items.title: The cobra effect is one of the more interesting phenomena in startups. Once you see it, you start noticing it everywhere
items.content:
The cobra effect is one of the more interesting phenomena in startups. Once you see it, you start noticing it everywhere, in your team, your metrics and now your AI agents.

It's basically when you reward people for hitting a number, and they find a way to hit it that makes the real problem worse.

The name "Cobra Effect" comes from a story about Delhi under British rule. There were too many cobras in the city, so the government offered a reward for every dead cobra people brought in. 

Instead of hunting them, people started breeding cobras so they could kill them and collect the money!

When the government found out and ended the program, the breeders let their snakes go, and Delhi ended up with more cobras than before!

I'm noticing that AI agents are making this more common. Basically, an agent will chase whatever number you give it, all day, without asking why. Tell it to make the tests pass and it might rewrite the tests. Tell it to close support tickets faster and it might close them without solving anything. It happens.

The best startups have already figured out the fix with people. Airbnb tracks bookings and host cancellations together. HubSpot takes back sales commission when a customer churns early.

The video breaks down how they did it, and it's the same playbook you'll want for your agents.

alright, before you open Claude again today. Read these 22 rules. Your weekly limit will thank you:

> Save your one free reset for a bad day.
> Use Opus 5.5 in every chat. Never Fable.
> Never switch models mid-chat.
> Never go back to an old chat.
> Ask for a 10-line summary and paste it in a new one.
> End quick questions with "No web search. No files."
> Plan your deck in text first. Ask for the file last.
> Highlight the part to fix, then click "Edit with Claude".
> Load your apps on demand (+ → Connectors → Tool access)
> Paste Anthropic's 2 sentences into Settings → General → Instructions
> Crop every screenshot. Turn every PDF into text
> Pause every scheduled task you don't read.
> Start every task with "Ask me questions before you start."
> Put all your asks in one message.
> Speak your prompts. I use Wispr Flow.
> Never correct Claude. Edit your prompt or start.
> One topic per chat.
> Keep your instructions under 2,000 words.
> Upload files you reuse once, in a Project.
> In Claude Code: one task, then /clear.
> Split your day into 3 sessions.
> Ask Claude for images. But rarely.

To copy Anthropic's 2 sentences (and see where to click for every rule), go to https://t.co/PAT8XFZobR

My favorite rule: limits reset every Sunday at 5 pm.

So Sunday is my Max day. I go extra crazy with Claude, on Extra or Max effort, and use up every token I have left before the reset.

PS: I’m not paid by Anthropic. My team hit the limit too many times before I figured this out.

Your kid's drawing on the fridge is one evening away from being a playable game hero. Claude Opus 5.5 handles the wiring

No 3D artist, no months in Blender, no grey capsule from a tutorial

It sounds like something only a game studio could pull off. A crayon drawing has no side view, no skeleton and no idea how to walk. But in 2026 every step between "drawing" and "playable" has its own tool, and Claude Opus 5.5 is the one that connects them

To Claude Code, your kid's hero is just a GLB file with bones and a few animation clips, and that's something it can wire into a game

Here's how it works:

> an image model redraws the drawing as a front-facing A-pose sheet that keeps every wobbly line, and Claude writes that prompt for you
> Meshy or Tripo turns the sheet into a 3D model on the free tier and exports it as a GLB
> auto-rigging gives it a skeleton, so the arms and legs finally know how to bend
> five clips are enough to feel alive: idle, walk, run, jump and one signature move
> Claude Code drops the GLB into a Three.js scene with a follow camera, WASD to walk, Shift to run and Space to jump

You can use it for a birthday game starring your kid's own character, a weekend project you build together, or a reason for them to draw the villain next

One honest note: free tiers often come with non-commercial terms, so check before you ship anything

items.content:
If you learn AI Security Engineering, you will never be unemployed again.

I’ll do this.

Stage 1: AI Attack Surfaces & Threat Modeling
- Learn:  OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, STRIDE for AI, the "Confused Deputy" problem in agentic workflows & data flow mapping.

- Practice:  Draw a complete threat model for an AI agent that reads emails and writes to a CRM, identifying every indirect injection and data exfiltration vector.

- Why:  You cannot secure an agentic workflow if you don't understand how an attacker can hijack the agent's legitimate privileges.

Stage 2: Advanced Prompt Injection & Jailbreaking
- Learn:  Direct vs. Indirect injection, Crescendo attacks (multi-turn grooming), payload splitting and encoding evasion (Base64, ROT13).

- Practice:  Build an automated harness that successfully bypasses a commercial LLM's system prompt using a multi-turn Crescendo strategy.

- Why:  Basic "ignore previous instructions" filters are trivial to bypass. Modern attacks groom the model's context over multiple turns.

Stage 3: Agentic Security & MCP Tool Poisoning
- Learn:  Model Context Protocol (MCP) security, JSON-RPC sanitization, shadow tool execution and least-privilege scoping for agents.

- Practice:  Write an MCP server that strictly validates incoming tool parameters via Pydantic and blocks "confused deputy" attacks where a user prompt tries to access admin tools.

- Why:  Agents are only as secure as the tools they call. Tool poisoning is the SQL Injection of the Agentic Era.

Stage 4: RAG Security & Data Poisoning
- Learn:  Vector DB access control, citation spoofing, shadow context injection and row-level security for semantic search.

- Practice:  Inject a "poisoned" document into a RAG pipeline that forces the LLM to output a specific malicious URL when queried about company policy.

- Why:  If an attacker can slip a poisoned document into your knowledge base, they own every answer the AI generates.

Stage 5: PII, Privacy & Cryptographic Guardrails
- Learn:  Deterministic masking, UUID swapping, differential privacy and pre-flight/post-flight unmasking proxies.

- Practice:  Build a middleware proxy that intercepts user prompts, swaps SSNs and credit cards for UUIDs before the LLM sees them and restores them post-generation.

- Why:  Compliance teams will kill any AI product that sends raw customer PII to a third-party frontier API.

Stage 6: Identity, Auth & Delegated Access for Agents
- Learn:  OAuth2 for machine identities, scoped JWTs, human-in-the-loop (HITL) approval gates and agent-to-agent (A2A) trust boundaries.

- Practice:  Build an auth broker where an AI agent acts on a user's behalf using a heavily scoped, time-limited OAuth token, rather than holding the user's raw password.

- Why:  Agents need hands but they should never hold the master keys to the enterprise.

Stage 7: Output Validation & Grammar-Constrained Guardrails
- Learn:  CFG (Context-Free Grammar) decoding, NeMo Guardrails, output sanitization and regex-enforced JSON schemas.

- Practice:  Implement a guardrail layer that physically prevents the LLM from generating markdown links or executable code blocks in its final output.

- Why:  You cannot rely on the system prompt to "please don't output bad things." You must enforce it at the token-decoding level.

Stage 8: Automated Red Teaming & Fuzzing
- Learn:  Microsoft PyRIT, Garak, LLM-based fuzzing, adversarial dataset generation and CI/CD security gates.

- Practice:  Build a CI pipeline using PyRIT that automatically attacks your agent with 1,000 adversarial payloads on every PR, blocking merges if the jailbreak rate exceeds 1%.

- Why:  Manual red teaming doesn't scale. You need automated, continuous adversarial fuzzing integrated directly into your deployment pipeline.

Stage 9: Model Extraction & IP Protection
- Learn:  Membership inference attacks, model inversion, API rate-limiting by semantic similarity and output watermarking.

- Practice:  Build an API gateway that detects and blocks scraping bots trying to extract your fine-tuned model's weights via thousands of systematic, low-temperature queries.

- Why:  Your fine-tuned model's weights are your IP. Competitors will try to distill your model through the public API.

Stage 10: Mechanistic Interpretability & Alignment Safety
- Learn:  Activation patching, logit lens, circuit discovery, detecting reward hacking and tools like TransformerLens.

- Practice:  Locate the specific attention heads in an open-source model responsible for "deception" or "sycophancy" and patch their activations to neutralize the behavior.

- Why:  You cannot fix hidden biases or misalignment if you treat the neural network as a black box. 

Stage 11: Compliance, Auditing & Governance
- Learn:  EU AI Act requirements, NIST AI RMF, immutable audit trails, SOC2 for AI and bias testing frameworks.

- Practice:  Build an immutable, append-only audit log that records the exact prompt, retrieved context, tool calls and final output for every single agent action.

- Why:  When an AI agent makes a mistake that causes financial or legal damage, the enterprise must be able to prove exactly why it happened.

Stage 12: Public CVEs, Teardowns & Portfolios
- Learn:  Responsible disclosure, writing security advisories, publishing threat models and bug bounty hunting for AI.

- Practice:  Find a vulnerability in an open-source AI framework (like LangChain or an MCP server), responsibly disclose it and publish a teardown of the exploit chain.

- Why: AI Security is a brand new field. Publishing novel attack vectors and defenses makes you the undisputed authority in the space.
